stories.headline: Punjab: In election season, bitter rivals are pals again
stories.title: Punjab: In election season, bitter rivals are pals again
stories.summary: BJP old-timers fear being sidelined twice over, by the Akalis and by turncoats queuing for tickets
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: In rural Punjab they say a quarrel between relatives lasts only until the next viah (wedding) in the family.

This Gurpurab, six years after Harsimrat Kaur Badal walked out of the Modi cabinet over the farm laws, Amit Shah and Sukhbir Badal joined hands at the BJP headquarters in New Delhi, signalling the Akali Dal’s return to the NDA.
It is also said that in Punjab politics, the photo album is always kinder than memory.
Sharing the frame with Shah and Badal was Ravneet Bittu, who not long back had said the BJP could not carry the Akali burden of drugs and sacrilege.
The surprise was Shah’s generosity.
The Akalis, he said, would remain the bada bhai.
He said the farm laws, over which Akalis had walked out of the NDA, no longer mattered since they were repealed.

Sukhbir called it “not merely a political alliance, but an emotional one”, invoked his father’s bond with Vajpayee and Advani, and announced that Prime Minister Narendra Modi would come to Moga on 8 December for Parkash Singh Badal’s birth anniversary.
Both sides spoke of Hindu–Sikh brotherhood, drugs and jobs.
It was the old Punjab, Punjabi, Punjabiyat script of 1996, dusted off for a new season.
But read the fine print.
No seat-sharing formula was announced.

stories.headline: Assam State Election Commission Sets December 9 for MaAC Draft Roll Release
stories.title: Assam State Election Commission Sets December 9 for MaAC Draft Roll Release
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: GUWAHATI: The Assam State Election Commission has announced that the draft electoral rolls for the upcoming General Election to the Matak Autonomous Council (MaAC) will be published on December 9, while the final rolls will be released on December 22.
The Commission issued a notification on Thursday directing the respective District Election.
Officers to prepare and publish electoral rolls for each constituency of the council, with January 1, 2026, as the qualifying date.
The electoral rolls will be prepared based on the delimitation notification issued by the Social Justice and Empowerment Department on November 21.
Relevant portions of the Assembly electoral rolls published by the Election Commission of India on February 10 will be bifurcated constituency-wise.

According to the schedule, master data entry and mapping of electors will be carried out from November 27 to December 1, while the inclusion and exclusion of electors will take place from December 2 to 8.
Claims and objections against the draft rolls can be submitted until December 15.
The Commission will dispose of all claims and objections by December 21 before publishing the final electoral rolls on December 22.
The state government has also reduced the prescribed period for filing claims and objections under the Matak Autonomous Council (Election) Rules, 2021.

stories.headline: US military says it disabled another ship that tried to breach naval blockade on Iranian ports
stories.title: US military says it disabled another ship that tried to breach naval blockade on Iranian ports
stories.summary: Washington, Nov 27: The US military has disabled a merchant ship in the Gulf of Oman that was trying to run its blockade of Iranian ports, US Central Command said Friday. A military aircraft fired “precision munitions” at the stern of the Palau-flagged M/V Pacific Archer on Thursday, and the "ship's propulsion was ultimately disabled and the civilian crew was unharmed,” it said in a statement. According to US Central Command, the Pacific Archer left the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas before it attempted to run the blockade. Ship tracking websites list the vessel's destination as Singapore. The strike comes as the Trump administration weighs its options in the long-simmering war with Iran, which began at the end of February and has settled into a quiet stalemate in the past several months. Earlier in November, officials in the region told The Associated Press that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was pushing the US to restart the war or allow Israel to launch airstrikes on Iran's nuclear facilities and missile capabilities. Meanwhile, government and security officials from the Persian Gulf countries, as well as Pakistan and Turkiye, were engaged in a diplomatic campaign, which included phone calls with senior US officials, to stave off a renewed war in the region. President Donald Trump has oscillated between threatening additional large-scale strikes on Iran and insisting that the war “militarily is effectively over.” The US military has maintained a sizable naval force in the region, including a constant presence of two aircraft carriers and a host of other ships. The US has been blockading Iranian ports since April, though the blockade was lifted in the summer during talks with Tehran and resumed in July. Since then, the US military says it has redirected 158 merchant ships and disabling those that refuse to comply. The Pacific Archer is at least the 15th disclosed vessel to be disabled by the US military since the blockade began in the spring and the sixth since it resumed this summer. The previous vessel was disabled on November 7. In June, the practice drew condemnation when a military strike on a Guinea-Bissau-flagged tanker attempting to evade the American blockade resulted in three deaths. Three Indian sailors were killed when American forces struck the Palau-flagged M/T Settebello, officials in India said at the time. The leader of the International Maritime Organisation, a United Nations agency, condemned the attack. US Central Command has consistently said that American forces issue multiple warnings before firing on the merchant ships. Iran's Revolutionary Guard said on Friday that two tankers attempted to transit the Strait of Hormuz through an “unauthorised” route, claiming that one of them struck a naval mine while the other was forced to turn back. The claims could not be independently verified. In a statement carried by Iran's state broadcaster, the country's Revolutionary Guard also said the number of oil tankers attempting to transit through unauthorised routes in the critical waterway has sharply decreased in recent days. Iran continues to warn ships not to pass through the strategic shipping lane without approval from Tehran. Oil flows in the first two weeks of November fell by around 20 per cent to around 13 million barrels per day compared with October, when exports roughly equalled the prewar amounts of 15-16 million barrels per day, according to Rystad Energy. Reasons for the November decline include Iranian attacks that discourage tankers from attempting the strait crossing and reduced flows through a key Saudi pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, which has also been attacked several times. A report by UN Trade and Development finds that disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, the Black Sea and the Panama Canal are lengthening voyages, raising fuel costs, driving port congestion and adding to uncertainty. Alternative ports, inland transport and logistics arrangements have kept trade moving, but at a higher cost.

stories.headline: Global South and Climate Justice
stories.title: Global South and Climate Justice
stories.summary: The Ministry of External Affairs website proudly and prominently mentions these words of Prime Minister Narendra Modi from his address to the 18th BRICS summit which was held in September this year under his chairship in Delhi “The Global South is today in the front row of global crises, but in the back row of decision-making. We must transform this “pyramid of privilege” into a “platform of partnership”, where every country has a voice, every member has a stake, and the advancement of humanity remains at the heart of every endeavour”. It has been India’s constant desire that the international system should be democratic and work for the welfare of the poor and underprivileged countries and peoples. It has championed the causes of the Global South and Modi has strongly moved in that direction too. But the sad fact is that the world order, put in place after the Second World War by the victors of that war, is essentially undemocratic. It has remained so for more than eighty years. Hence, the question is whether Modi’s aspiration will ever get translated into reality. Or, is the Global South consigned to play little or no role in decision making on issues which are vital for its future. Apart from the desire of the advanced countries to retain rules making powers for inter-state relations and thus deny the Global South a role in this area, the absence of consensus within it on some vital global matters hampers it from pressing its case for eroding the “pyramid of privilege”. Once again this came to the fore in the Conference of Parties (COP) 31st meeting of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) which concluded earlier this week in Turkiye without a main outcome document. This was one of the few occasions when a COP meeting ended on this note. This was not a good augury for finding a resolution for the principal existential crisis facing humanity–that of climate change. In any event, as this writer has noted in these columns, the absence of the US from the UNFCCC makes it weak. This is because the US is one of the highest emitters of greenhouse gases (GHG The principal reason for the collapse of COP 31 was the failure of the parties to reach an agreement on the phasing out of fossil fuels. On the one side were some advanced countries and some developing island states which favoured an aggressive approach while on the other were countries, including India, which wanted a realistic attitude and not to mention a phase out of fossil fuels. The Indian statement focused on the real causes of climate change. Bhupinder Yadav, Minister for Environment put it well when he said ““Our planet is warmer today. The cause is the industrialisation and economic growth of some, fuelled over two centuries by unabated greenhouse gas emissions. To now expect the Global South to bear the burden of addressing the consequences of their past actions in the name of ‘higher ambition’ is unjustified’. He also correctly remarked “Developing countries cannot be asked to choose between climate action and the legitimate right to development, to decent living standards, health and education. Equitable access to the remaining, depleted, carbon budget is non-negotiable”. Yadav’s words were justified for countries like India but small island countries like Maldives or some in the South Pacific fear that even a little rise in sea levels because of global warming would lead to their doom. It is this survival instinct which compels them not to heed the call for climate justice that countries like India push for. These divergent interests in the ranks of the Global South are exploited by advanced countries to break its unity. That is one point that Modi could have addressed in his BRICS address and that leads to the diplomatic task that India could perform. This relates to seriously embarking on an exercise to create a unity in Global South countries on major issues which will increase their bargaining power. Another objective that India could lead is to increase the fund of scientific and technical capacities of these countries. One obvious way of creating unity in the Global South on climate change because of global warming, is to focus on the need of the advanced world to adhere to their pledges on adaptation and mitigation. Indeed, India could suggest that a larger per capita proportion of this assistance could be given to island countries because the threat they face is existential. Besides, they have small populations and that forward looking international conventions must be framed for their welfare and rehabilitation, including political, in different parts of the world. This concern is not based on an unrealistic scenario for a rise of even a metre in sea levels could submerge some island countries in the South Pacific which are really a string of atolls. As it is India has a dialogue with the South Pacific Forum. The idea expressed here could be refined and taken forward to ensure that the unity of the Global South on climate change is restored. Another area where India could build on is to imaginatively share its expertise with the Global South in applications relating to AI which are being developed here. Such cooperation will be in keeping with the tradition established in the early years of its independence when Indian experts went out to developing countries to share Indian experiences and developing countries students came here to study. Now the circumstances have changed but new ways have to be found to take that process forward.

stories.headline: Tata Sons vs Tata Trusts: Caveats filed in Bombay HC, Supreme Court ahead of crucial November 30 board meeting
stories.title: Tata Sons vs Tata Trusts: Caveats filed in Bombay HC, Supreme Court ahead of crucial November 30 board meeting
stories.summary: Tata Sons has filed caveats in the Bombay High Court and Supreme Court after Tata Trusts failed to secure interim relief. The November 30 board meeting will proceed, but its decisions remain subject to the final court order.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
event term: 'supreme court' in summary weight 26.4
article_sentences: Under Section 148A of the Code of Civil Procedure, a caveat safeguards a party against an ex parte order being passed without giving it an opportunity to present its arguments.
On Friday, Justice Abhay Ahuja of the Bombay High Court declined to grant interim relief to Tata Trusts, which collectively holds a 66% stake in Tata Sons.
The court scheduled the next hearing for January 21, 2027.
While the decision allows Tata Sons to proceed with its scheduled November 30 board meeting, resolutions passed during the meeting will remain subject to the final outcome of the litigation.
Two constituent entities of Tata Trusts — Sir Dorabji Tata Trust (SDTT) and RD Tata Trust (RDTT) — approached the court on Thursday, challenging Chandrasekaran’s reappointment for a third term.
The trusts also sought restrictions on the upcoming board meeting, whose agenda includes a proposed listing of Tata Sons.

At the centre of the legal battle is Section 121 of Tata Sons’ Articles of Association (AoA), which governs additional voting requirements involving nominee directors of Tata Trusts and the chairman’s casting vote.
During the September 17 board meeting, Noel Tata, chairman of Tata Trusts and a nominee director on the Tata Sons board, opposed Chandrasekaran’s reappointment.
Venu Srinivasan, the other nominee director, supported the proposal.
The split between the two nominee directors prompted acting chairman Harish Manwani to exercise his casting vote.
All other board members supported Chandrasekaran’s reappointment.
Tata Trusts has argued that a split between its nominee directors means the requisite affirmative majority has not been secured.

stories.headline: India's FY28 fiscal deficit projected to stay unchanged at 4.3% of GDP: Deutsche Bank
stories.title: India's FY28 fiscal deficit projected to stay unchanged at 4.3% of GDP: Deutsche Bank
stories.summary: Deutsche Bank warns FY28 consolidation faces rising pay, subsidies and oil-linked costs, even as cushions keep the deficit at 4.3% of GDP
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: India's fiscal deficit for the financial year 2028 is projected to remain unchanged at 4.3 per cent of GDP as expenditure pressures challenge consolidation efforts, according to a Deutsche Bank Research report.
While the central government is on track to meet its fiscal deficit target of 4.3 per cent of GDP in FY27, the path forward presents steeper hurdles.
"The central government will most likely meet its FY27 fiscal deficit target of 4.3% of GDP; however, FY28 consolidation looks considerably more challenging.
Considering the various risks, we forecast the FY28 fiscal deficit to remain unchanged at 4.3% of GDP," the report stated.

Several cushions support the government's fiscal math in the current fiscal year, including a substantial Reserve Bank of India dividend of ₹2.9 lakh crore, an ₹1 lakh crore Economic Stabilisation Fund provision, potential capital expenditure compression, and higher-than-expected disinvestment receipts.
However, the subsequent fiscal year faces headwinds from persistently elevated oil prices, larger subsidy bills, a potentially lower central bank dividend, and the rollout of the 8th Pay Commission.
"Implementation of the 8th Pay Commission, which could add at least ₹3 lakh crore to expenditure.
Delaying the pay award to 2028 could provide near-term relief but would merely shift the burden forward through a larger accumulation of arrears," the report noted.
Despite fiscal and external challenges, the report maintains a steady view on economic expansion.
Real GDP growth is projected at 7.3 per cent year-on-year in FY27, 7.2 per cent in FY28, and 7.3 per cent in FY29.

Although a sub-normal monsoon, higher oil prices, and unfavourable base effects from last year's GST rate cuts are expected to moderate growth in the second half of FY27, the implementation of pay commission awards is anticipated to lift domestic demand next year.
"We remain broadly constructive on India's growth trajectory and general resilience of the economy despite the ongoing West Asia crisis and a sub-normal monsoon this year," the report added.

stories.headline: Why Kashmir must heed the Uttarakhand warning
stories.title: Why Kashmir must heed the Uttarakhand warning
stories.summary: Viral videos showing heavy earthmoving machines cutting into the fragile shoreline of Sheshnag Lake in upper Pahalgam have sparked deep environmental concern across Jammu and Kashmir. Located at around 11,780 feet, this excavation is not a routine project, but a serious threat to the ecological and water security of South Kashmir. Objections from the Kashmiri Pandit community and civil society groups also highlight the religious and cultural value of this alpine landscape. Subjecting a sensitive glacial lake to heavy mechanical digging ignores both its ecological fragility and spiritual sanctity. In its defence, the Border Roads Organisation stated that the machinery is widening and stabilising existing tracks, easing Amarnath Yatra congestion, and following environmental safeguards. While improving pilgrim access and managing crowds are valid administrative goals, the methods used must respect mountain geology. High altitude terrain comprises unstable glacial deposits, loose moraines, permafrost, and steep slopes that fail easily when disturbed. Heavy excavation without scientific assessment worsens erosion, weakens slopes, and alters natural water channels. An ecosystem cannot be stabilised by weakening its geological foundation. Experiences across the Indian Himalayan Region offer clear warnings. The Kedarnath disaster and land subsidence in Joshimath exposed the heavy cost of development that exceeds natural limits. Uttarakhand has since faced intense scrutiny over carrying capacity, crowd management, and construction in fragile zones. These lessons must guide planning across the Himalayan arc, including Kashmir. The real question is not whether pilgrims need better facilities, but whether they can be provided without harming the natural systems sustaining entire populations. The danger at Sheshnag is acute because of its location within the upper Lidder glacial landscape. Experts have listed Sheshnag among 14 high risk glacial lakes in Jammu and Kashmir prone to Glacial Lake Outburst Floods. Such floods occur when natural barriers holding back glacial water suddenly fail. Disturbing moraines, altering drainage channels, or weakening nearby slopes increases existing risks. Devastating glacial lake floods in Sikkim and other Himalayan regions demonstrate why preventive action must precede environmental damage. The consequences extend well beyond the lake's shores. Together with the neighbouring Kolahoi glacier system, the Sheshnag basin feeds the upper Lidder River, which flows through Pahalgam and Bijbehara before joining the Jhelum near village Gur. This river is indispensable for drinking water, irrigation, farming, and South Kashmir's wider economy. Its waters support extensive paddy cultivation, horticulture, local trade, and tourism across Pahalgam, Bijbehara, Anantnag East, and nearby areas. Weakening this upper catchment threatens a shared resource supporting thousands of households. Scientific evidence makes these concerns urgent. Research led by noted Earth scientist Professor Shakil Ahmad Romshoo, Vice Chancellor of the Islamic University of Science and Technology in Awantipora, highlights the rapid retreat of regional glaciers. In a 2020 study of 147 glaciers across the Kashmir Himalaya, including the Lidder, Vishav, Doodhganga, and Sind basins of the Jhelum River, Romshoo and colleagues found a 28.82 percent area loss between 1980 and 2018, shrinking from 101.73 square kilometres to 72.41 square kilometres. Mapping South Kashmir glaciers like Kolahoi, Hoksar, and Wokhalbal, the study revealed that smaller glaciers under one square kilometre lost 41.20 percent of their area compared to 15.97 percent for larger glaciers above three square kilometres, while fragmentation split 11 glaciers and raised the mapped count from 147 to 153. Complementing these findings, a 2020 study by Irfan Rashid and colleagues on the Kolahoi Glacier documented a 23.6 percent area loss between 1962 and 2018, with retreat rates tripling after 2000. Their research shows shrinking ice has significantly reduced Lidder River flows at Aru, Gur, and Kirkadal, pushing downstream farmers to cut water intensive rice paddy cultivation by 39 percent while orchards and built up areas expanded sharply. Rising temperatures alongside vehicular emissions, ambient black carbon, pilgrim crowds, waste, and excavation place severe stress on this corridor, reflected in the premature melting of the natural ice lingam and eroding slopes. The legal framework is equally clear. The Supreme Court and the National Green Tribunal have consistently stressed precaution, scientific scrutiny, and accountability in ecologically sensitive zones. Under the Precautionary Principle, authorities must prevent serious or irreversible environmental harm even when scientific uncertainty persists. Any major alteration around Sheshnag must follow transparent environmental appraisal, geological and glaciological studies, and statutory clearances. Administrative promises of safeguards cannot replace independent scientific verification. The administration need not choose between pilgrimage and environmental protection. Both can coexist if development respects natural carrying capacity. Heavy mechanical digging in the Sheshnag and upper Lidder catchments must stop immediately until independent glaciologists, geologists, and environmental scientists evaluate slope stability, moraine integrity, drainage patterns, downstream flood exposure, and cumulative ecological impacts. Their findings must enter the public domain to guide a strict carrying capacity framework and monitoring system. A pilgrimage acquires deeper meaning when nature is protected rather than sacrificed for convenience. The Himalayas are living ecosystems, not endless construction sites, sustaining rivers, agriculture, biodiversity, and communities far beyond their boundaries. Uttarakhand has paid a heavy price for overlooking these limits, and Kashmir must not repeat those mistakes. Safeguarding this fragile landscape is inseparable from protecting South Kashmir's water security and future generations. The author is a serving legislator from South Kashmir’s Bijbehara constituency and contributes occasionally on public policy and governance.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Extends Interim Bail Of Khalid Saifi and Tasleem Ahmad In Delhi Riots Larger Conspiracy Case
stories.title: Supreme Court Extends Interim Bail Of Khalid Saifi and Tasleem Ahmad In Delhi Riots Larger Conspiracy Case
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court on November 27 extended the interim bail granted to Khalid Saifi and Tasleem Ahmed, who are accused in the 2020 Delhi riots larger conspiracy case.
They were earlier granted interim bail for 6 months, which has now been extended by 3 more months.
A bench comprising Justice Kumar and Justice Vipul M Pancholi passed the order.

It may be recalled that a bench comprising Justice Aravind Kumar and Justice P. B. Varale granted interim bail to them on May 22, considering the long period of incarceration undergone and the reference to a larger bench due to the "perceived conflict" on the interpretation of the 2021 K. A. Najeeb judgment.

stories.headline: Supreme Court orders Karthigai Deepam to be lit at ‘deepathoon’ on November 28; issues contempt notice
stories.title: Supreme Court orders Karthigai Deepam to be lit at ‘deepathoon’ on November 28; issues contempt notice
stories.summary: Bench directs Tamil Nadu Chief Secretary, DGP, Madurai District Collector, temple authorities to be present for next hearing on Dec. 15; court sees ‘pre-meditated conspiracy' between State and temple trustees
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: Rejecting the Tamil Nadu government’s claim that it stayed aloof from the Arulmigu Subramaniaswamy Temple management’s customary decisions, the Supreme Court on Friday (November 27, 2026) said non-compliance with its November 20 order to light the Karthigai Deepam at the deepathoon (stone pillar) atop the Thirupparankundram hill in Madurai amounted to “wilful disobedience” born of a “pre-meditated conspiracy” between the State and the temple trustees.

A Bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M. Pancholi ordered the Board of Trustees of the temple to be suspended before appointing two former High Court judges – former Chief Justice of Meghalaya High Court S. Vaidyanathan and former Madras High Court judge Justice V. Parthiban - to act as Receivers.
The court directed the Karthigai Deepam to be lit again on Saturday (November 28, 2026), this time on the stone pillar, as was originally ordered on November 20.
Central forces would provide security.
The Receivers have to ensure the ceremony is carried out in consultation with the temple stanikars.
However, the interim order would not grant any future equities in favour of any party.
The court made clear that its order was limited only to contempt petitions.
The main case on religious rights concerning the Thirupparankundram lamp-lighting row would be heard in the second week of January 2027.
The row stems from the claims of ownership over the hilltop.
The deepathoon is located near the Sikandar Badusha Dargah on top of the hill, while the Arulmigu Subramaniaswamy temple is at the base of the hill.
The dargah side has claimed ownership of the hilltop, including the deepathoon site.
The court order comes two days after the ceremonial lamp was lit at the customary location – Deepa Mandapam – atop the hill and not as the Bench mandated.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Refuses Urgent Hearing on Plea Challenging Ramayana Film's Portrayal
stories.title: Supreme Court Refuses Urgent Hearing on Plea Challenging Ramayana Film's Portrayal
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Friday declined to entertain an urgent listing request in a petition challenging the portrayal of the Hindu epic Ramayana in a movie, observing that there was no reason for immediate judicial intervention as the film had already hit theatres.

A bench of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana made the observation after the petitioner's counsel sought an early hearing, alleging that the movie presented a distorted account of the epic.
Pointing out that the film was already running in cinemas, the CJI remarked that those interested in watching it had already had the opportunity to do so.
"The movie has already been released.
People who wanted to watch, they have already seen," the CJI said.
The petitioner's counsel argued that the film contained several factual distortions which could influence the younger generation.

The bench, however, was not persuaded by the submission and, responding to the objection, said filmmakers were entitled to present the epic from their own perspective and that anyone holding a contrary interpretation could express it through their own creative work.
"They have made a movie as they understand.
You make your movie as you want.
Don't waste time of the court.
If you have a counter-view about the epic, you make a movie on the counter-view," CJI Kant remarked.

stories.headline: Assam Cabinet approves two new reserve forests, Rs 252 crore in industrial investments
stories.title: Assam Cabinet approves two new reserve forests, Rs 252 crore in industrial investments
stories.summary: The proposed reserve forests will cover 12.49 hectares at Purachapori in Nagaon district and 5.6 hectares in the Nokhuti-Nongte area of Lumding.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'cabinet approves' in title weight 44
article_sentences: GUWAHATI: Assam is set to get two more reserved forests (RFs).
With this, their number is set to go up to 314.
Currently, there are 312 notified RFs in the state with 17,864 sq km area.
Chaired by Chief Minister Dr Himanta Biswa Sarma, the Assam Cabinet approved the proposal for creation of the two new RFs on Friday.

While one forest reserve will be created in Burachapori, Sonitpur district over an area spanning 12.49 hectare (ha), the other will come up in Nakhati, Lumding in Hojai district and spanning 6.5 ha area.
Incidentally, both the proposed RFs will be created in the areas that were freed from encroachers by authorities.
Of course, the Chief Minister clarified before the media that public hearings will be conducted, before formally notifying the two RFs.
The cabinet also approved Rs 145 crore approved for giving scooties to higher secondary (HS) students securing 80% and above.
Each scooty has been estimated to cost the state exchequer Rs 80,000.
Two investment proposals worth Rs 253 crore were also cleared by the cabinet.
While Gangwal Healthcare Private Limited has submitted a proposal to make an investment worth Rs 152 crore in Tinsukia, Godrej Group has proposed Rs 101-crore investment in Cachar.
The cabinet also approved allotting 35 acre land at Panchgram in Cachar district to Godrej Group for palm oil cultivation.

stories.headline: New quota bill proposes 50 per cent increase in seats, freezes delimitation till 2051; April bill left both open
stories.title: New quota bill proposes 50 per cent increase in seats, freezes delimitation till 2051; April bill left both open
stories.summary: New Delhi, Nov 28: The Constitution (132nd Amendment) Bill, 2026, slated for introduction in Parliament next week, proposes a 50 per cent increase in Lok Sabha seats and a freeze on delimitation until 2051 to facilitate the implementation of women's reservation. The proposed legislation marks a significant departure from the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, introduced in April, which had sought to facilitate the implementation of women's reservation but provided neither for an increase in the number of seats nor for an extension of the delimitation freeze. The bill was defeated in the Lok Sabha for want of the required two-thirds majority. The changes come against the backdrop of strong opposition from southern states, led by the DMK, to the earlier delimitation proposal. The party argued that states which had successfully controlled population growth should not be penalised through a reduction in their relative representation in Parliament. The DMK has maintained that Tamil Nadu's existing 7.18 per cent share in the Lok Sabha should not be reduced in any expansion of the House. It has also insisted that the relative proportion of parliamentary representation among states, based on the 1971 Census, should remain protected for another 25 years. The new bill retains the 1971 Census as the basis for allocating Lok Sabha seats among states, while providing for the redrawing of constituencies within states based on the latest published census figures. It proposes raising the maximum strength of state assemblies from 500 to 650 and the Lok Sabha ceiling to 850, comprising 815 seats for states and 35 for Union Territories. Unlike the April bill, the latest proposal provides for a uniform 50 per cent increase in seats across states and Union Territories, while extending the freeze on inter-state allocation until 2051. This is intended to address concerns that population-based delimitation could alter the existing balance of representation between states. The DMK's support has emerged as an important factor in the government's efforts to secure the special majority required for passage of the constitutional amendment.
